title: Why did the little helicopter on Mars stop flying?
blurb: Ingenuity flew 72 times on Mars. Then it crashed. Engineers worked out why, from 100 million miles away, with no one there to see.

cover.alt: The small Ingenuity helicopter standing on reddish Martian ground, with part of the Perseverance rover in front.

source.name: NASA
source.title: NASA Performs First Aircraft Accident Investigation on Another World

cards.b: Ingenuity was a tiny helicopter, about 49 centimetres tall. It travelled to Mars under the Perseverance rover, a robot car that drives around on another planet. Ingenuity was the first aircraft to fly on another planet. It was planned to fly 5 times, but it flew 72 times, over almost three years. On its last flight, its blades broke. What went wrong?

Engineers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California, with the company AeroVironment, studied the last flight. Håvard Grip was Ingenuity's first pilot. Teddy Tzanetos was the project manager at the end. MiMi Aung led the project when Ingenuity first flew in 2021. They shared their findings in December 2024.

Nobody was there to see it, and a plane's black box, which records a flight, was missing. So the team studied the data and pictures Ingenuity sent back. Ingenuity found her way with a camera that looked down at the ground. It tracked pebbles and bumps, the way you watch the road go by from a bus window. On the last flight, the ground below was smooth sand ripples, which are small wavy hills made by wind.

img.alt: A black and white view from above of smooth, wavy sand ripples on Mars, with the helicopter's shadow.

cards.b: About 20 seconds into the flight, the camera could not find enough bumps on the smooth sand to follow. So Ingenuity got her speed wrong. She landed while still sliding sideways, and hit the slope of a ripple hard. She tipped and rolled. All four spinning blades snapped near their tips.

img.alt: A drawing showing the helicopter coming down, hitting a sand slope, tipping over and losing parts of its blades.

cards.b: The team says this is the most likely story, not the only possible one. They had only the helicopter's own data and photos. Other things could have happened too. A later photo from the rover showed a broken piece of blade lying about 15 metres away, which fits their story.

Air on Mars is very thin, about one hundredth as thick as ours. Ingenuity proved a helicopter can still fly there. Now engineers know future helicopters need better ways to see smooth ground. NASA is already planning a bigger Mars helicopter that could carry science tools to places rovers cannot reach.

Test what Ingenuity's camera found hard. Put a plain white sheet of paper on a table. Look straight down at it, close enough that it fills your view, while someone slides it slowly. Can you tell how fast it moves? Now draw dots all over it and slide it again. Is it easier to tell? Smooth sand has nothing to follow, as the plain paper has none. Bumps and pebbles are like the dots.

Ingenuity was planned to fly only 5 times. The team kept flying her until she broke. Was that brave, or risky? One view says you learn the most by pushing until something fails. Another says you should stop while things still work. Which would you choose?
